evidence.text: The transplant office was on the fourth floor of the city hospital at Fennick Street, four miles and one long walk across the river, and Mara went on the eleventh day with her papers in a bread wrapper so they would not get wet. A clerk sat behind a grille with rimless spectacles and a stack of folders, and she was kind, which was the worst of it — she took the clinic letter and read it, and she asked about Lio in a voice that had asked about other children that morning.
"The course is eleven thousand eight hundred marks," the clerk said. "Half on admission. The surgeon's fee is separate and I would not insult you by pretending otherwise."

evidence.text: Tomas had not put his mask back on properly since the first day. He wore it, but he wore it wrong: one strap, then the other, seated loose, so that at the sides he could feel the room come in. She had watched him do it for a week before she said anything, and when she did say it he said his skin was raw and the strap cut him, and turned his face away.

He was sitting on the third step with his back against the wall and his mask hanging from one ear, breathing slow and deep through his open mouth like a man drinking. His hands were in his lap and they were shaking, and his eyes were closed, and on his face was a look she had not seen there in years — a slackness, a softness, the easing of a man who has set down something heavy.

He opened his eyes. For a moment he was going to lie; she could see him reach for it. Then his face came apart. "Minutes," he said. "At first minutes. In the night. Just to sleep. Mara, I can't sleep, I can't — I lie there and my skin crawls and my heart goes and it's like being held under water."

"I know." He put both hands over his face. The tremor ran through his wrists. "I know what I am. I knew it before the masks. I've known it since I was twenty and my back went and the only thing that made the mornings bearable was that the air made them bearable. I never had to say it out loud before. That's the gift, isn't it. That's what the masks have given me — I have to say it out loud."

evidence.text: The fifth day taught Calder Row the sound of itself. Every breath in the tenement now passed through a vent that clicked, and the clicking came through the walls and up the stairwell, a thousand small mechanical throats clearing at once. Mara lay awake and listened to it. Tick, tick, tick. Under it, the one that did not click at all — Lio's, wet and shallow, turning over in the room next door like a stone in a pocket.

Sober, she had learned, did not mean clear. It meant she felt everything at its actual size. The cold was colder. Four flights of stairs were four flights, and by the third landing her thighs burned, and she remembered that once she had floated up them. The grief was the same. The grief had not shrunk; she had simply stopped being carried past it, and now she had to walk through it every morning to reach the landing.
Lio got worse.

It was not a crisis — Mara knew the crisis now, she had held it in her arms on the cobbles — it was slower and worse than that. The mask kept his body working, but it made him work for it. Each breath had to be taken, deliberately, like a stair. He sat at the window with his hands in his lap and his chest going up and down and the gray coming back around his mouth, and by the end of the week he had stopped asking to go down to the street.
"Only when I think about it," he said. "So I don't."

evidence.text: The laundry yard had no soap and no coal. On the second day the carts had stopped coming, then the water had gone to a trickle at the standpipe, then the district office had posted a notice that said deliveries were being reorganized and asked for patience in a font so small it looked ashamed. Nel from the dye house had stood in the yard with her arms folded and said, "They're punishing us," and nobody had argued, because the men in gray had known about the gas and the masks had come anyway, and now the shelves at the chandler's were bare and the bread line started at dawn and did not move.
The yard did not open.

"What other way." She kept her voice level. She had learned on the stairs that she could keep it level now, that the rage had settled into something she could carry. "The yard is shut. The shelves are empty. There is no work and there is no credit and there is no one in this district with twelve thousand marks except the men who put the gas in the air. Tell me the other way, Tomas. Say it out loud. You couldn't put your mask on. You've been breathing the Lull in the stairwell to get to sleep. So say it out loud."

evidence.text: My ult ticks. Eleven seconds. Nine. Four.
It comes up, and the horn sounds in my head, and I don't press it.

That's the hardest thing I've done tonight. The key is in my hand. The door is right there — Renekton at the front of the wave with his stun up and his Baron buff glowing, Sable behind him, Pyke somewhere in the fog with his hook. And I hold it, because full-damage Rengar into a Baron-buffed front line is a suicide note with a build path. Renekton has a stun and a heal and armor I can't cut through in one rotation. I land on him, I do eleven hundred damage, he survives at a third, and then the entire enemy team knows exactly where I am and exactly how long my ult has left.
So I hold it and watch the turret drop.

evidence.text: The screen goes grey at the edges and the horn sounds low in my ears and there's a charm coming over the wall.

Pip's charm. Over the wall. She comes through the jungle entrance at a dead sprint — a mid laner arriving twelve seconds into a fight she isn't supposed to be in — and throws it at the fog where the back half of their team is standing, and it hits two. Pyke. Sable. Both of them caught in the pink, walking forward into nothing, and Sable's distortion is at one second and it doesn't matter because she's charmed.

intent.brief: Chapter 3 of 6, "Fifteen Minutes." Continue first-person present tense on Rook exactly where chapter 2 ended: waiting, ult at zero, third and final super wave spawning, all four enemies off the map at Baron, Pip at 12:40 into her disconnect. Beats: (1) They take Baron — purple buff on all four — and the third super wave crashes into the base with the Baron wave behind it; the defense is losing, a nexus turret drops low, Bess is still holding top wave but about to rotate. (2) Rook's ult comes up but he cannot spend it into a Baron-buffed front line; he holds it, and the tension is the clock. (3) At exactly the fifteen-minute mark Pip's wireframe turns green mid-fight — "Pip has reconnected." She types an apology, Nox answers with a number, and she immediately calls enemy summoner timers from memory (Renekton Flash, Pyke hook/flash, Sable's cooldowns) in a whisper, giving Rook the one opening he needs. (4) Bess finally abandons her finished wave ("the tray's done") and lands the Ornn engage; Pip's charm over the wall catches two; Rook's ult deletes Draven as he tries to cash in — the fourth key. (5) Clean fight: four enemies dead, Renekton limps away, base cleared, Baron now up for the taking. End with Pip starting a long apology in chat and deleting it, and Rook saying one word to her. No resolution of the game yet.

scores.goal: 招募Pip屋顶侦察员、Doreen医护、Cass爆破农夫

evidence.text: "Well." He jerked his head at the shed. "I got a hundred pounds of ammonium nitrate, forty feet of galvanized pipe, and a bad idea. Come see the bad idea."

Pip came down off the shed's gutter like a spider being lowered on a string, dropped the last six feet, and landed in a crouch she'd clearly practiced in front of a mirror. Sixteen. Wiry, windburned, wearing a climbing harness over a coat two sizes too big.

"I'm the one on the silo." She said it the way you'd say *I'm the one who walked on the moon*. "Sixty-two of them at the brewery as of this morning. Sixty-two I can count. There's more inside the shed, I can hear them in there moving around, but the roof's peeled and you can't see in from the ladder. You can from the silo. I go up at first light and again at four."

Doreen Ash arrived at dusk, on foot, carrying a canvas bag and smoking, which meant she'd walked a half mile through open ground with a lit cigarette in her mouth and nothing had eaten her, and that told me more about her than anything she said for the next hour.

She laughed, flat, one syllable, like a door closing. "All right. I'll take it. I don't care what's in your flask as long as your hands are steady when it counts and you don't hand me a job I can't do. I've got a notebook. I write down everybody I treat. Then I write down everybody I lose." She tapped the bag. "I've had this book six months. I'm on my third one. You want to know the worst thing about the end of the world? It's the paperwork."

"Then you'd better find one," I said, "because you're the only one of us who can read that field from above, and I'm not sending a man up that rope with a bad hip. You're the scout. Not because you're fast. Because you're the only one who can see."

"Right. But somebody's going to be at the tank when it blows. Somebody's going to be holding that hose in the mud while the rest of us get clear." He wasn't grinning now. "So before I get my hands in the fertilizer, I need to hear you say it plainly, because I've been on a farm crew when the water came up and nobody wanted to say it, and I've seen what happens when nobody says it."

evidence.text: The cemetery lay on the way to everything, which was one of the reasons Dave had agreed to the house.

His walk to the print shop took him along the bottom of the hill, and the iron fence ran with him for two hundred yards, black and sooty and taller than it needed to be. Beyond it the ground climbed away under leaning stones. The mist came off the hill most mornings and stood in the low parts until nearly ten, and on the days it did the whole place looked like a room somebody had left the door open on.

He had walked it eleven days now, and on the twelfth the mist was thick enough that the far fence was a rumour. Near the gate, in a plot he had come to know by its neighbours — a squat granite lamb on one side, a leaning cross on the other — the ground was dark and turned. A rectangle of it, six feet by three, the turf cut back in neat sods and stacked at the head end, and the earth beneath dark and wet and otherwise undisturbed.
No stone. No flowers. No machine tracks in the gravel.

Dave stopped with his hands in his coat pockets. He was a man who restored maps for a living, and one of the things you learned doing that was that a thing which has been changed tells you where the change begins. This change began at the edge of the sods and ended there.

evidence.text: He had noticed it before, and he had not said it aloud, not to Mira and not to himself in any words he kept: when the mist lay like this, the shapes behind the fence kept pace with him.

Not one shape. Three or four, upright, dispersed among the stones at the far edge, moving when he moved and stopping when he stopped. He could see them in the corner of his eye, tall dark suggestions with the mist moving through them.
He looked straight at them.
Mist. A yew tree. The corner of a mausoleum with green running down its face. Nothing standing anywhere.
He walked on, and the shapes came back into the side of his vision, keeping pace, four of them, unhurried.

He tried it three ways. Looking straight — nothing. Looking at his feet and counting his steps — the shapes slid along in the margin, patient as a tide. And then, at the comer, when he turned his head fast without committing his eyes, he caught one of them half-turned away, going, a smear of shade the height of a man and no more substantial than a smudge on glass, gone before he could make it a person.

evidence.text: Mira came down at eight with her headphones round her neck and found him at the stove, and said, "You've got the face of a man who's been chatting with headstones."
"Say hello to the dead for me tomorrow." She lifted her glass an inch. "Tell them Mira says they could use a gardener."

He laughed. It came out fine — he heard it come out fine — and then it kept going a half-beat too long, and something in the kitchen changed temperature in a way that had nothing to do with the house.
"It was a small joke," she said, quieter. "You're laughing like I hit you."

"It's a cemetery, Dave. There's always earth." She put her glass down, and not gently. "I'm going to finish the Foley pass. There's a scene where a man walks down a corridor for four minutes, and honestly it's more restful than this."

She went up, and the headphones went on, and Dave stood in the kitchen with the sauce and the smell of it and the knowledge, unwelcome and precise, that he had told her the true thing and she had heard only the mood he was in.

evidence.text: **1.1(b) — Thread Sovereignty.** The player who posts first in a thread owns the thread. Ownership is absolute, permanent, non-transferable, and carries no privileges of any kind.

I want to sit with that last part, because it took me a while. Sovereignty, in the Committee's usage, is not control. It is attribution. You own the thread the way a person owns the weather they were standing in.

Example. In March I posted: "does anyone else's ceiling fan sound like a helicopter or is that just mine." Six upvotes. Then a stranger replied, "it's the bearings, you idiot," and got three thousand. Under 1.1(b) I own that thread. Under everything else, I own a ceiling fan that sounds like a helicopter and a permanent public record of being called an idiot by a person whose username is a number.

[4] 1.1(b) entered the codex in v2.6 after a landmark dispute over a thread about sandwiches. The Committee ruled that the thread belonged to the player who had posted the word "sandwich" and then never returned. That thread remains open. The sandwich remains undefined. There are now four hundred and eleven replies and no sandwich.

evidence.text: **1.1(c) — The Lurker's Exemption Clause.** A player who never posts cannot be scored.
I know. I know. Read it again. It does not say "cannot be penalized." It says *scored*, and the Committee's grammar is not sloppy, it is load-bearing.

My brother has lurked for eleven years. He has never posted, never commented, never voted. He reads the feed the way other people watch weather — with mild interest and no intention of going outside. His karma is zero. Under the Clause, zero is *inviolate*. He is the only person I know who is technically safe, and he is safe because he does not exist to the scoreboard. He is not winning. He is not losing. He is filed.

[5] Full title: "Lurker's Exemption (Non-Participation as a Form of Victory) (Provisional)." The word "Provisional" has been pending review since v2.9. Nobody has reviewed it. Nobody is going to review it. The reviewer position has been vacant for six patches and there is, I am told, a hiring freeze across the afterlife.
And here is the thing that kept me up. If the only protected state is not existing on the scoreboard, then the Committee is not offering safety. It is offering deletion, with a footnote.

evidence.text: **1.1(d) — The Ratio Doctrine.** The truth value of a statement is equal to its upvote-to-downvote ratio, calculated hourly, retroactively, and in perpetuity.

Example. In April I correctly stated that the 14 bus does not run on Sundays. I had the schedule. I had a photograph of the schedule. A reply guy with forty thousand followers informed me that the 14 bus runs on Sundays, "actually," and that people like me were the reason public transit was dying. His comment went to eleven thousand. Mine went to negative two hundred, because the ratio does not measure who read the schedule. It measures who arrived first with the more satisfying feeling.
The 14 bus does not run on Sundays. I know this because I stood in the rain on a Sunday. The rain did not get upvotes either.

[6] Under the Doctrine, the Committee once corrected a factual error in an official post by pinning a comment to the top. The pinned comment was downvoted. The error is now canon. It appears in Appendix K, between the recipes for soda bread and something called "funeral potatoes."

evidence.text: Every sub-rule so far can be satisfied by being *seen*. Not one of them can be satisfied by being *right*. Correctness is not a scored category. There is no field for it. I checked. I checked the survey from the ninth ticket cycle and there is one question and it is not about accuracy.

The cat in the tiny hat posted a photograph this morning. Just the photo. No caption, no comment, no follow-up, nothing but a cat and a hat and the general concept of a hat. Four hundred thousand upvotes. The cat has never filed a ticket. The cat has never been wrong because the cat has never been right because the cat has never been *about* anything. The cat is the purest player in the zone.
And I do not think it is an accident that the cat is ahead of me. I think the cat is the *design*.

Because the cat has never been right about anything. The cat has merely been seen. Four hundred thousand times. That is the whole game, and I have finally read the rules well enough to lose it on purpose.

evidence.text: Sub-rule 1.1(b)(iii): "Sovereignty is permanent. Ownership of a thread may not be transferred, revoked, or shared, and in the event of conflict with any other sub-rule, this clause prevails."
Sub-rule 1.1(d)(iv): "Ownership of all threads and statements belongs to the crowd, which may reassign it hourly; in the event of conflict with any other sub-rule, this clause prevails."

Both paragraphs are on the same page. Both are in the same font. Both are stamped **BINDING** in bold, and I have checked, and the stamps are not decorative — decorative stamps are a different stamp, they are italic.

A thread belongs permanently to whoever posted first. And a thread belongs to whoever the crowd decides hourly. At the same time. Forever. Both binding. Both prevail. Two absolute claims in one document, in one subsection, and the Committee has not marked either as provisional, which it did for a footnote about lurkers that has been pending since v2.9.
Then I did the only thing a player can do with a contradiction, which is to feed it a test case and see which clause bills me.

Tomorrow, 9 a.m. I am going to post the exact same sentence into two threads. In the first, I will be the original poster and the sentence will be stupid. In the second, I will arrive late and the sentence will be identical and the sentence will still be stupid. Under 1.1(b) I own the first thread forever. Under 1.1(d) the crowd owns both from the first hour. One of these clauses will have to give, and the Committee will have to tell me which one in a way that is timestamped and witnessed by at least three strangers who do not like me. If they cannot, then I have found the seam.
Bring two snacks tomorrow. One of them is going to be scored, and I would like it to be yours.

Two control wards. He spent half his ammunition on her. He'll never say why and neither will I.

evidence.text: I'm already moving, because I've been watching the map the way you watch a bill come due — Sable's been off the wave for eleven seconds, she's not in the river, and the only reason a LeBlanc leaves a lane she's winning is that she's found something to flank.

Chain, sigil, the full rotation, the thing that deletes a carry in one and a half seconds flat, and Mags' health bar goes nine, then four, then three, and stops at three, because the shield ate it.

I press R.
Empowered Q. One rotation: leap, Q, and she's gone before the second half of the animation, and the shutdown gold hits my account in a fat gold tick.

evidence.text: The depot had been a tram shed once, and it still smelled of grease and cold iron under the sharp sterility of the disinfectant they were spraying every hour. Jonah sat at the long table with the log terminal ticking to itself, and the city came to him in numbers.

Mask serial 44-9012, fitted at the Calder Row gate, first breath at 9:14, heart rate one hundred and forty, then falling. 44-9013, a woman of sixty, no reading at all for six minutes, then a spike that would not come down. 44-9014, a boy of eight. He knew the number without looking it up. He had written it himself in the ledger, in ink, with a thumb that had been smeared blue all morning.

Behind him the shed doors stood open on a street that had stopped being a street. A cart lay on its side in the road with one wheel turning slowly, and beyond it the tram wires hung down in loops, and somewhere past the chandler's a fire was going that nobody had come to put out. The sirens had been going since noon and had begun to sound less like sirens than like weather.
When it eased he stood up and went back to the logs.

The work was the only thing that helped. There was a way of holding the numbers at arm's length: this one lived, this one didn't, this one had torn the mask off in the street and would have to be found and refitted, and if not refitted would seize within a day. He flagged them. He wrote notes. His hand was still unsteady and his writing had gone ugly, and he kept writing.

evidence.text: He got up and took a mask from the case. 44-1388. He seated it, pinched the metal bridge over his nose, checked the seal with his palm and a hard breath in, and then he breathed.

The first thing was the smell coming back. Not a smell — the absence of one. All his life the air had had a weight to it, a softness at the back of the throat like the taste of a room where someone has been sleeping, and he had never known it was there because it had never not been there. Now it was gone and the shed was only a shed: grease, iron, cold, disinfectant, the wet wool of Halvorsen's coat as she passed.
The second thing was his hands shaking.

He sat down on the bench with the mask clicking softly against his face and the tremor running up his forearms like a held note. His heart knocked. Sweat came out along his hairline and went cold. And underneath all of it, arriving the way a tide arrives, was a feeling he had no name for except that it was the opposite of being carried, and it said, very quietly, you did this to them, and you did not have to, and you cannot take it back.
Then his hands wanted the mask off.

The want was not a thought. It came from the wrist and the throat and the back of the skull and it said: lift the straps, just for a moment, just to wet your mouth, just to breathe the way you have breathed every day of your life. He sat on his hands. He counted the ticks of the terminal. He thought about his mother's kitchen, and about the fact that he was thirty-one years old and had never once, in his whole remembered life, felt this tired.

evidence.text: There was a case of masks at the end of the row, unclaimed, serial numbers consecutively inked. He had fitted two hundred and eleven of them in one day. He had put his hands on two hundred and eleven faces and told each of them the same thing: the first minutes are the worst, sit down afterward, don't try to walk far. He had said it kindly. He had believed he was being kind. He had gone home at night with his own lungs full of the ordinary air of the city and slept eight hours and got up and done it again, and it had never once occurred to him — not once, not in the whole long year of training and briefing and signing the forms that said he understood the purpose of the program — that he had been handing out the first sober breath of anyone's life without ever having taken one himself.

The first thing was the smell coming back. Not a smell — the absence of one. All his life the air had had a weight to it, a softness at the back of the throat like the taste of a room where someone has been sleeping, and he had never known it was there because it had never not been there. Now it was gone and the shed was only a shed: grease, iron, cold, disinfectant, the wet wool of Halvorsen's coat as she passed.

He sat down on the bench with the mask clicking softly against his face and the tremor running up his forearms like a held note. His heart knocked. Sweat came out along his hairline and went cold. And underneath all of it, arriving the way a tide arrives, was a feeling he had no name for except that it was the opposite of being carried, and it said, very quietly, you did this to them, and you did not have to, and you cannot take it back.

He gripped the edge of the bench and breathed through it. In and out through the vent, which clicked, which was the only sound he allowed himself. He had told Mara Voss it would steady. He understood now what a cheap thing that had been to say. It steadied the way a fever steadies, by burning through.

evidence.text: It was three in the afternoon when he pulled the next file, and the file was wrong.

Lio Voss, age eight. That was ordinary. Clinic letter, diagnoses, the wet cough, the gray mouth. He had read it standing at the gate with the boy's mother's eyes on him, and he had read every line because he always read every line and because there was something in her face that made him want to be the kind of man who read every line.

But the file in the terminal was not the clinic letter. It was the district health index version, and it had a header on it that he had seen in training and had never seen on a live intake. A red bar. A code. PRIORITY TRANSFER — DONOR-FAMILY FAST TRACK. Under it, a program number, and under that, a line of text in the flat grey language of people who had stopped hearing themselves: potential registrant, mother; household debt profile; projected payment sufficient for full transplant course; eligibility window ninety days.

Nobody had explained to him that the files of sick children in poor districts were being tagged before their mothers had said a word. Nobody had explained the phrase fast track. He was not a stupid man. He felt the shape of the thing under the words, and the shape of it was a hand already reaching into a coat pocket, folding a contract, refolding it until the crease went soft.

evidence.text: Halvorsen called after him about his shift. He lifted a hand and did not turn around.

The street outside was not a street. It was a held breath gone wrong. Glass lay in the gutters in long glittering fans, and the smell of the fire had reached even through the vent, sharp and chemical and almost clean. Three blocks on, a gang of men had stopped a city cart and were throwing the crates down into the road, and the crates burst and the masks spilled out and went skittering underfoot, and nobody picked them up. A woman sat on a doorstep with hers in her lap, turning it over and over like a thing she had found and could not identify.

He walked. The mask made the walk strange; the air was too thin and too cold and his legs did not feel like his own, and twice he had to stop at a wall and put his hand on the brick until the tremors passed. Wanting to take it off. Not taking it off.

At the corner of Calder Row the tenements rose up gray against a gray sky, laundry lines strung between them and nothing on the lines, and he could hear the district from here — not a riot, not any more, but a low grinding sound, people talking all at once in doorways, a child wailing somewhere high up, a handcart going over broken glass.
He put his hand flat over his coat, where the folder was.
Then he went down into the Row.

evidence.text: There was a case of masks at the end of the row, unclaimed, serial numbers consecutively inked. He had fitted two hundred and eleven of them in one day. He had put his hands on two hundred and eleven faces and told each of them the same thing: the first minutes are the worst, sit down afterward, don't try to walk far. He had said it kindly. He had believed he was being kind. He had gone home at night with his own lungs full of the ordinary air of the city and slept eight hours and got up and done it again, and it had never once occurred to him — not once, not in the whole long year of training and briefing and signing the forms that said he understood the purpose of the program — that he had been handing out the first sober breath of anyone's life without ever having taken one himself.

He sat down on the bench with the mask clicking softly against his face and the tremor running up his forearms like a held note. His heart knocked. Sweat came out along his hairline and went cold. And underneath all of it, arriving the way a tide arrives, was a feeling he had no name for except that it was the opposite of being carried, and it said, very quietly, you did this to them, and you did not have to, and you cannot take it back.
He read it three times. He was aware, in the way you are aware of a noise in another room, of his own breath clicking in the vent.

He thought, more honestly, standing in a tram shed with his hands shaking and a want in his chest like a dog at a door: I cannot be a man who does nothing, and I am too much of a coward to be a man who reports it.

evidence.text: It's bigger than our minions, that's the thing nobody tells you. It comes in with a little gold cape and a health bar like a turret and it does not care about anything. Behind it: a normal wave, then a second super, then the enemy creep line stretched all the way back to where our inhibitor used to stand. Renekton is somewhere in that fog. Lee Sin we can't see at all, which is worse. Pyke's ult sound is the scariest thing in the game and it is off cooldown.
"Twenty-one seconds on Renek's Flash," Bess says, flat, like she's reading a bus timetable. "Lee's got Smite up, he'll be on Baron side. Let it come to us. Plated."

That's why I have the clock. Every enemy flash, in order. Renekton's is already back up — Bess called it at twenty-one before the wave hit, and the wave ate forty seconds — so that's one more thing I can't jump into. Pyke's is down — Bess called it, seventeen seconds, then "up" — no, "up" was Lee. Pyke's down for another forty. And Draven, Draven of the enormous ego and the two spinning axes, Draven has Flash. Draven has always had Flash.
Draven is walking out of their jungle into mid with an axe in the air.

The axe lands. He catches it. Another spawns. He's rotating through the wave to farm Adoration stacks, and he's doing that thing Draven players do where he walks three steps past his own creep line and lets his support cover him, and this time Pyke is not there. Pyke is at the Baron pit. Lee Sin is at the Baron pit. Renekton is just now leaving mid.

evidence.text: **Rook:** mid.

Pip doesn’t clear her throat, doesn’t apologize first. “Draven twenty-six,” she whispers. “Pyke twenty-nine. Sable twenty-two. Lee Sin twenty-five. Renekton’s not on a timer, he’s — he’s in the river, he’s going home, he’s at eight hundred health.”

Here’s what I know about their Lee Sin. He doesn’t clear the river with the team. He goes ahead, alone, to ward the flank, because a Lee Sin who isn’t sneaking is a Lee Sin who’s already lost. The brush by our red buff is where he does it. It’s where he did it at eight minutes and at fourteen and it is where he will do it now, because people do not change in twenty-two minutes, they just get more expensive.

Their draft is finished. It’s done. It was built to end the game at fifteen minutes, and it is now twenty-three, and the parts don’t fit anymore. Renekton’s damage falls off a cliff past twenty — he was a threat when our turret was at twelve percent and he could stun Mags and delete her, and now he can’t frontline because he dies in one rotation the second he walks up. Sable’s full combo can’t kill through Nox’s shields; I watched it land on Mags at three health and do nothing, and it will do nothing every time, because a LeBlanc with no follow-up is a spectator with a hat. Draven needs Adoration stacks and he needs them so badly he’ll take three steps past his own creep line for them, and a Draven three steps past his line is a Draven I can kill five times. Pyke’s execute only works on somebody below the threshold, and the only person on our team who goes below the threshold is Mags, and Nox has been pulling her out of it all night on a half-second lantern.

Our mid inhibitor is still rubble. It has been rubble since before I respawned twenty minutes ago, and it means the lane has no door, and so the Baron-buffed line walks in through the broken wall and the super minions walk in with it, gold capes, turret-sized health bars, and they hit the last nexus turret.

evidence.text: The folder had a routing number on the inside flap, stamped in faded violet under the fast-track bar, and Jonah had looked at it for four days before he understood that he was going to follow it.

He waited until the depot emptied. The night clerk knew him and did not look up from his paper as Jonah signed the records room key out; night shift was three men and a terminal, and nobody counted the keys. The vault smelled of cold paper and dust and the disinfectant they still sprayed at the change of every shift. He sat on a stool under a single bulb with the Voss folder open and the manifest ledgers stacked beside him and went through them page by page, the way he had been trained to go through everything.

He found it in the third book. A tissue consignment, logged the day after the masks went out, listed under the fast-track program and addressed not to the city hospital but to the State Hygiene Directorate, Ardith Street works, Bay Four. He traced the line back and forward. Every fast-track registration in the Calder district fed the same address. Every one. Marrow, tissue, and the small gray word *donor* repeated down the column like a drumbeat.

The Ardith Street works was a long low building behind a fence with a gatehouse and a boiler chimney that put up no smoke. Jonah went at the change of shift, in his gray, with his mask seated properly and a cold-chain inspection form he had filled in himself, in his own neat hand, because he kept meticulous records and a meticulous record was a thing nobody looked past.

Bay Four was cold enough that his breath plumed inside his mask. Crates stood on pallets, each stenciled with the same violet routing stamp he had found in the vault, and each with a paper slip zip-tied to the handle. He crouched beside one and read the slip. *Donor Lot 117-C. Post-harvest, viable, transfer to synthesis.*

evidence.text: CONTINUITY — SUSTAINED-RELEASE COMPLIANCE AGENT — PHASE II.
Under it, smaller: *Synthesized from viable donor tissue. Single administration. Non-reversible.*

Two technicians came past him with a cart and did not see him. One was saying, "—because the air was never the product, the air was the *delivery*," and the other laughed and said, "The air was *wasteful*," and they went on through the door with the cart.

The Lull had been in the air because the air was free and could not be measured and could not be billed. It wore off. It was a soft thing, a carrying-thing, and softness was expensive to maintain. But the files said the masks were never the cure. The masks were the *triage*. And the donors — the poor, the desperate, the mothers with sick children and ninety days — the donors were not research material. They were the first batch, and the compact was how you got a population to pay for its own compliance in instalments of flesh.

"It's what comes next." She said it without heat. "You've seen what the masks did to the Row. Forty thousand people breathing through a filter with no job and no bread and no gas and nothing to hold them down. You think that was a cure? That was a wound. We have been holding this city up with a soft gas for two generations and you handed every one of them a knife and told them to cut themselves free." She tapped the desk. "Continuity is the same service, delivered properly. Once. Permanently. No vents, no masks, no withdrawal. And yes, it's built from donor tissue, and yes, the donors are the first to receive it, because the donors are already inside the system and because the tissue is theirs and because nobody is going to march for them. That's not a conspiracy, Reyes. That's *population management*. Somebody has to do the arithmetic."

evidence.text: "Then you know you've committed a falsification and an unauthorized entry, and I could have your card by noon." She turned her cup a quarter turn. "Sit down, Reyes."

She let that sit. Then she said, "You have a mask log, Reyes, and a stolen file, and a falsified form. I have your career in a drawer. I can take your card and your pension and your address, and I can have your mask reissued with a monitoring flag, and you will be a man in a gray coat standing at a gate for the rest of your life, and none of it will make a single difference to Bay Four." She set the cup down. "Or you can go back to your table and do your job, and I will forget this morning."
Halvorsen looked at him over her mask. "Somebody has to process the paperwork," she said. "It may as well be someone who reads every line."

evidence.text: He recorded it.

He did it properly, in the records room, over two nights, with the door locked and the bulb burning. He copied the manifest lines. He wrote out the Ardith placard word for word. He wrote down what the two technicians had said, and what Halvorsen had said, and the exact hour she said it, because he kept meticulous records and because a record was the only thing he had ever known how to make. He put it all in a sealed envelope, addressed to the only editor at the *Calder Register* whose name he knew, and he carried it in his coat for a week.
He could not send it.

He told himself it was the monitoring flag, the card, the pension. That was true and it was not the reason. The reason was the woman on the cobbles with both hands pressed over her son's mouth, and the ninety days running, and the fact that if he sent this envelope the Directorate would close the program and burn the files and the Voss boy would die in a room with a wet cough and a gray mouth, and Jonah would have been right, and it would have saved nothing.
He put the envelope in the drawer with the Voss folder and closed it.

evidence.text: On the sixteenth day the transfer order came down from Halvorsen's office without a note: *Reyes, J. Reassigned to Donor Intake. Effective immediately. Family caseload, priority.*

He set his log terminal up at the intake desk at four in the afternoon. The chair was different. The bulb was the same. He entered his code and the first record dropped into the queue before he had taken his coat off, and he sat looking at it for a long moment with his hands flat on the desk.
VOSS, MARA. VOSS, LIO — PROGRAM FAST TRACK. REGISTRATION: PENDING. COUNSELOR: REYES, J.

The appointment was for nine in the morning. He would be the one to open the door. He would be the one to lay the compact flat on the desk and turn it around and walk her through the terms in the flat gray language, and to say the word *irrevocable* out loud, to her face, and to explain what she was agreeing to.

evidence.text: He sat with his thumb on the line and listened to his own vent click.
Jonah stood in the cold with his clipboard against his chest and felt the shape of it close like a hand.
He stood in the doorway and said, "You put the file in front of me. You knew what it was."

He did it properly, in the records room, over two nights, with the door locked and the bulb burning. He copied the manifest lines. He wrote out the Ardith placard word for word. He wrote down what the two technicians had said, and what Halvorsen had said, and the exact hour she said it, because he kept meticulous records and because a record was the only thing he had ever known how to make. He put it all in a sealed envelope, addressed to the only editor at the *Calder Register* whose name he knew, and he carried it in his coat for a week.

He told himself it was the monitoring flag, the card, the pension. That was true and it was not the reason. The reason was the woman on the cobbles with both hands pressed over her son's mouth, and the ninety days running, and the fact that if he sent this envelope the Directorate would close the program and burn the files and the Voss boy would die in a room with a wet cough and a gray mouth, and Jonah would have been right, and it would have saved nothing.
